title: What is Learning -3
author: Martin Skelton
summary: In this instalment of his series defining learning, Skelton focuses on the brain's heavy energy demand and how it shapes learning. He uses personal examples, including a draining day of interviews, to show that mental work consumes a large share of the body's energy. The brain therefore saves energy by pruning unneeded capacities, by pattern matching, and above all by hardwiring repeated experiences until they become automatic. He argues practice makes permanent, not perfect, illustrated by reaching for a moved shower squeegee for five weeks. He closes with a revised working definition: learning is the brain extending chains, making constellations more complex and hardwiring repeated chains.
points: The brain uses roughly thirty percent of daily energy, so it has evolved to economise and avoid new effort wherever possible.
Pruning, pattern matching and myelination of frequently fired neuronal chains are the main energy-saving mechanisms.
Practice makes permanent rather than perfect, so repeated wrong experiences are learned just as well as right ones.
Unlearning and relearning cost energy, which explains why old habits resist change even when we know better.
The post offers a revised definition of learning as extending chains, increasing complexity and hardwiring repeated experiences.
quotes: A functioning brain demands around 30% of our total daily energy supply. Without this level of supply, the brain functions more slowly, is less able to handle complexity and/or stops functioning at all.

Energy is a competitive resource for our brains. As a result, they have evolved to become energy savers. As the Beatles sung many years ago, the brain has become hard-wired to take ‘the easy way out’ when it can.
Why would the brain do this? Because it saves energy to focus only on what the brain appears to need.

Imagine the brain’s energy requirements if it had to treat every experience as brand new every time. It would get depleted very quickly. Patterns and matching - finding that something is like something else, even if not completely accurate - use up much less brain energy than treating everything as though it were different from everything else.

Becoming automatic by hardwiring repeated experiences is one of the most important ways the brain significantly reduces the amount of energy it uses so that it can deal with all of the new stuff coming its way. It’s the new stuff that requires attention, and attention requires energy. Hard-wired automatic responses, not so much.
Practice doesn’t make perfect. Practice makes permanent. Paradoxically, we can learn ‘wrong’ things very well.

Here’s TAKEAWAY 2 - a still incomplete but further revised version of our embryonic definition of ‘learning’. Learning happens successfully when, after the appropriate development has taken place, our brains a) extend an existing neuronal chain, b) make a neuronal constellation more complex and c) hardwire a repeated existing chain so that it fires automatically.
